newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Yeltsin gives Chubais role in tax clampdown.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Yeltsin gives Chubais role in tax clampdown.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin promised to clamp down on tax evasion on Friday and gave one-time reform chief Anatoly Chubais a key role in a new commission to oversee the task.

Yeltsin, speaking clearly in a radio address apparently recorded in the Barvikha sanatorium, said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin would head an extraordinary commission on taxes and the budget and Chubais would be his deputy.

"I know taxes are high in Russia today, but we will be able to lower them only if we manage to ensure compliance with tax legislation," said Yeltsin, who faces an operation in the next two months to improve blood supply to his heart.
"First we collect taxes and then we will cut them."
Yeltsin made clear that better tax collection was the only way to raise enough money to pay off a huge backlog of wages to pensioners, servicemen and workers in the state sector.
"Those who dodge taxes make pensioners, the army, science and culture eke out the life of semi-paupers," he said.

The new commission, which will oversee the activities of the customs and tax services, will continue Chubais' comeback on to the Russian political scene. RIA news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying its first meeting would be next week.
Yeltsin sacked ginger-haired economist Chubais unceremoniously in January, but brought him back into his administration in July as Kremlin chief-of-staff.

Chubais, 41, had masterminded Russian privatisation, dubbed the biggest sell-off of state property in history. He took charge of Russian economic reforms when pioneers Yegor Gaidar and Boris Fyodorov left the government.

Tax evasion and wage arrears are two of the biggest problems facing the economy today and taxes are the main concern of the International Monetary Fund, which has extended Russia a three-year $10 billion loan.
The money, being paid in monthly tranches, is being used to help close the budget deficit.
Parliament, dominated by communists, is debating the 1997 budget on Friday.
Deputies are expected to reject the draft, which envisages a deficit of 3.3 percent of gross domestic product, and the government will then have 20 days to come up with new proposals.
This year's tax revenue is already lagging well behind budget levels and the State Tax Service said last week that tax revenues fell 29 percent in September from August levels.
In September the government collected only 45 percent of budgeted taxes while taxes for the first nine months of the year were running at only 75 percent of budgeted levels, it said.
The government has already tried to rake in taxes from some companies. Monopolist gas producer Gazprom said last week that the officials had frozen several bank accounts.
Gazprom admits it is behind on tax payments, but says its customers owe it much more than it owes the government.
Economists said Yeltsin's intervention might help ease the problem of tax collection.
"It is certainly good that people at the highest level are giving a lot of attention to this issue," said Tom Wolf, resident representative with the IMF in Moscow.

He said a new IMF mission was expected to arrive in Moscow next Wednesday for their regular monthly review of the Russian economy. Tax issues and budget plans for 1997 would both be on the agenda, he said.
